questions.question: What is the requests library and how do you make GET and POST requests?
questions.title: The requests Library: GET and POST
questions.direct_answer: requests is Python's standard HTTP library (the human-friendly alternative to urllib). GET retrieves data (requests.get(url, params=...)); POST sends data to be processed (requests.post(url, data=... or json=...)). A Response object gives you the status code (.status_code), the body as text (.text), the body parsed as JSON (.json()), and the headers (.headers). requests handles URLs, encoding, redirects, and cookies for you — it's the go-to for HTTP in Python.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know GET vs POST (retrieve vs send), the Response object's main attributes (status_code, text, json(), headers), and that requests handles encoding/cookies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using POST for a read operation, or not checking the status code / not knowing .json() exists.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: GET retrieves (requests.get, params= for query string); POST sends (requests.post, data= or json=). Response gives .status_code, .text, .json(), .headers.

sections.title: requests Is the Human-Friendly HTTP Library
sections.content: requests is Python's standard HTTP library — the human-friendly alternative to urllib. It handles URLs, encoding, redirects, and cookies for you, so you can focus on the request and the response. GET retrieves data: requests.get(url, params={'q':'x'}) where params adds the query string. POST sends data to be processed: requests.post(url, data=form_dict) for form data, or requests.post(url, json=payload) to send JSON and set the content-type automatically. The Response object gives you .status_code (the HTTP status), .text (the body as a string), .json() (the body parsed as JSON, raising on non-JSON), and .headers (the response headers).

sections.title: GET vs POST and the Response
sections.content:
GET retrieves with params; POST sends with data/json; the Response carries status, body, and headers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G[requests.get\(url, params\)] --> R[Response]
  P[requests.post\(url, json\)] --> R
  R -->|status_code| S[200/404/500]
  R -->|text / json\(\)| B[body]
  R -->|headers| H[headers]
```

sections.title: A GET and a POST request
sections.content:
```python
import requests

# (1) GET: retrieve data. params= adds the query string.
r = requests.get('https://api.example.com/users',
                 params={'active': 'true'}, timeout=10)
print(r.status_code)        # 200
print(r.json())            # the body parsed as a Python list/dict

# (2) POST: send data. json= sends JSON and sets content-type automatically.
r = requests.post('https://api.example.com/users',
                  json={'name': 'Ada', 'age': 36}, timeout=10)
print(r.status_code)       # 201 (created)
print(r.json())            # the created resource

# (3) FORM DATA: use data= instead of json=.
r = requests.post(url, data={'field': 'value'})

# The Response object: .status_code, .text, .json(), .headers, .cookies
```

sections.title: GET vs POST and Response Attributes
Common Mistakes
items: Using POST for a read-only operation (GET is correct; POST may have side effects).
Not checking the status code — assuming success; a 4xx/5xx still returns a Response.
Not knowing about .json() — parsing .text with json.loads when .json() does it for you.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: requests is Python's standard HTTP library; GET retrieves, POST sends.
GET: requests.get(url, params=...) where params adds the query string.
POST: requests.post(url, json=...) sends JSON (and sets content-type) — or data= for form data.
Always pass a timeout; check .status_code (a 4xx/5xx still returns a Response, not an exception).

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: requests is Python's standard HTTP library, the human-friendly alternative to urllib. It handles URLs, encoding, redirects, and cookies for you, so you can focus on the request and the response. GET retrieves data — requests.get of url with params for the query string. POST sends data to be processed — requests.post of url with data for form data or json to send JSON and set the content-type automatically. The Response object gives you status_code, the HTTP status; text, the body as a string; json, the body parsed as JSON which raises on non-JSON; and headers, the response headers. The common mistakes are using POST for a read-only operation where GET is correct and has no side effects, not checking the status code because a 4xx or 5xx still returns a Response rather than raising, and not knowing about dot json — parsing dot text with json.loads when dot json does it for you. Always pass a timeout so a hung server doesn't block you forever.
